# 1 Welcome {data-name="Welcome"}

## 1.1 Teaching machines to read DNA

- 28 letters of one RNA sequence bound by the protein AGO2, and the same letters as numbers
- A CNN trained on such sequences gives the full 330-letter sequence a score of **0.81**. What in the sequence produced that number?

![](assets/custom/hero.png){fig-align="center" height="399px"}

::: {.notes}
Presenter: Mattan.

- The CNN the participants train in an hour reads the whole sequence and returns 0.81.
- The question for every model today: what in the sequence produced the score?
- The data are RNA (letters A, C, G, U). The DNA models later in the day read the same sequences with T in place of U.
:::

::: {.center}
# 2 The biology {data-name="Biology"}
:::

## 2.1 The seed rule

- AGO2 carries a microRNA. Its **seed** (letters 2 to 7) pairs with the target mRNA; this site also pairs letter 8

![](assets/custom/seed_pairing.png){fig-align="center" height="432px"}

::: {.notes}
Presenter: Roee.

- DNA is transcribed to messenger RNA, which is translated to protein. AGO2 acts on the messenger RNA.
- AGO2 carries a microRNA of about 22 letters. The seed pairs with the mRNA (A with U, G with C, antiparallel). Where AGO2 binds, the mRNA is degraded or not translated.
- The top row is a real bound sequence from our data. It contains the miR-16 site UGCUGCU, which pairs with microRNA letters 2 to 8.
- More than 60% of human protein-coding genes carry conserved microRNA sites (Friedman et al., Genome Res 2009). A single-letter variant in a site can create or remove regulation, for example the let-7 site in KRAS (Chin et al., Cancer Res 2008). siRNA drugs such as patisiran work through AGO2.
- An experiment covers one cell type and one condition. A model can score transcripts, variants and designed sequences nobody measured, provided it learned the rule.
- Hypothesis for the day: a model that learned AGO2 targeting should respond to seed sites like this one. Slot 3 tests it.
:::

## 2.2 The data

- **Bound**: about 48,000 sites where CLIP-seq found AGO2. **Unbound**: about 44,000 random positions in the same genes

![](assets/custom/labels_raster.png){fig-align="center" height="596px"}

::: {.notes}
- CLIP-seq: UV light crosslinks proteins to the RNA they touch, an antibody pulls down AGO2, and the attached RNA fragments are sequenced.
- The data set is the GraphProt CLIP benchmark (Maticzka et al. 2014), used by Pan and Shen (2018). Each sequence is about 330 letters, with the measured 40-letter site in the middle (letters 150 to 190 in almost every sequence) and context on both sides.
- Each row is one sequence, each pixel one letter: dark for G or C, light for A or U. 150 of each class, sorted by G+C. The white stripes on the right are sequence ends (sequences differ in length).
- The bound block is slightly richer in A and U: mean G+C 0.42 vs 0.46 in this sample, 0.41 vs 0.45 over all 92,000. AGO2 sites are often in AU-rich 3′ UTRs, so part of this may be biology, and part may come from how the unbound positions were drawn. Slot 7 tests that.
:::

::: {.center}
# 3 Learning and testing {data-name="Learning"}
:::

## 3.1 What training does

- Model: $\;\hat p = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$, with $x$ = (G+C fraction, U fraction)
- Training: compute the gradient of the loss, move $w, b$ against it, repeat

![](assets/custom/lr_training.png){fig-align="center" height="584px"}

::: {.notes}
- The smallest possible model on our data: two features per sequence and three parameters. The line is where the predicted probability equals 0.5.
- The Slot 2 CNN has 2,491 parameters. The genome models have millions to billions.
- The loss is binary cross-entropy; a coin flip gives 0.69. Here it falls from 0.77 at a deliberately bad start to 0.67. The two numbers carry some information; Slot 6 measures how much.
- The sigmoid $\sigma$ maps any score to a probability between 0 and 1. Every model today ends with one.
:::

## 3.2 Train, validate, test

- **Train**: fit the parameters
- **Validation**: choose settings such as the number of epochs
- **Test**: report once; never used for choices
- Slots 2 to 6 use the same **1,000 held-out sequences** as the test set; Slot 7 builds new test sets

::: {.notes}
- Never grade a model on the data it was trained on.
- Slot 2 prints the held-out AUROC after every epoch, so we do look at the test set during training. That is acceptable for a workshop as long as nobody picks the best epoch by it; in a real project that is the validation set's job.
- The split is random by sequence. We checked for near-duplicates: 47% of held-out bound sequences have a training sequence within 150 letters on the genome (13% of unbound). On the 698 held-out sequences without one, the CNN scores 0.85 instead of 0.86, so the effect on our results is small. Real projects split by gene or chromosome.
:::

::: {.center}
# 4 Reading a result {data-name="Results"}
:::

## 4.1 AUROC

- **AUROC** = the probability that a random bound sequence scores higher than a random unbound one. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.

![](assets/custom/auroc.png){fig-align="center" height="596px"}

::: {.notes}
- Left: the CNN's scores on the 1,000 held-out sequences, bound in blue and unbound in grey.
- Each threshold on the left gives one true positive rate and one false positive rate, one point on the right. The area under the curve is the AUROC.
- It does not depend on a threshold, so it compares models fairly. It says nothing about why a model scores well.
- For the Medical Diagnostics students: this is the ROC of a diagnostic test, sensitivity against 1 minus specificity.
:::

## 4.2 Noise in a held-out AUROC

- On 1,000 test sequences, 95% of resampled AUROCs fall within about **±0.025**

![](assets/custom/auroc_ci.png){fig-align="center" height="642px"}

::: {.notes}
- Resample the 1,000 test sequences with replacement 2,000 times; the bar covers 95% of the resulting AUROCs.
- Three models from today: the CNN (0.86), logistic regression on 5-letter word counts (0.74), and on the two composition numbers of 3.1 (0.66). The bars do not overlap: these are real differences.
- The bars describe one model at a time. Two models scored on the same sequences make correlated errors, so their difference varies less than the bars suggest; a paired bootstrap measures it. Overlapping bars mean no evidence of a difference, not proof that the models are equal.
- Rule of thumb: on 1,000 test sequences ignore differences below about 0.03; on 3,000 (Slot 7), below about 0.015.
:::

## 4.3 Fit vs held-out

- Report the held-out score; a large gap to the training score means the model memorised its training data

![](assets/custom/probe_trap.png){fig-align="center" height="596px"}

::: {.notes}
- The same model, logistic regression on 5-letter word counts, scored two ways.
- Left: 12,000 training sequences with regularisation. 0.82 on its own training data, 0.74 held out. A small gap is normal.
- Right: 600 sequences and almost no regularisation. 1.00 on its training data, 0.67 held out.
- This is the first thing to check in any evaluation code, including code an AI assistant wrote: which data was the score computed on?

Next: Slot 2, build the CNN.
:::
